newsitem.title: USA: Dreyfus Corp sees US Treasuries rally ending soon.
newsitem.headline: Dreyfus Corp sees US Treasuries rally ending soon.

text.p: The rally in U.S. Treasuries could be ending soon, while the market should continue to have significant volatility in 1997, said Kevin McClintock, head of taxable fixed income at the Dreyfus Corporation.

"We're close to the end of the rally. The next 20 basis points will be harder to get than the last 25 basis points," McClintock said at Dreyfus' year-end market outlook on Tuesday. "We're looking at (bond) rates heading up in the first quarter."

He noted that economic news is starting to turn stronger and that holiday shopping should be healthy. "I can see market participants worrying about stronger growth and then start to price in a (Federal Reserve) tightening" early next year," McClintock said.

Treasuries don't offer as much value as other bonds, he said. "Our focus is on newer types of securities," he said, specifically naming commercial and residential mortgage backed bonds, asset backed securities, adjustable rate mortgage (agency and non-agency) and high-yield as fixed-income values.
Corporate bonds, he said, are overbought and, like Treasuries don't offer as much value as the others.
McClintock, who manages four Dreyfus funds, said that he has recently taken on a neutral to a bit of a long position.
He added that he forsees the Fed on hold through at least the first quarter of 1997.
Meanwhile, Richard Hoey, chief economist at Dreyfus predicts U.S. economic growth in 1997 at about trend, with a Fed "stuck on neutral" through midyear and with a dollar rising slightly more.
Hoey, though, predicts the Fed will raise short-term rates by a half-point in the second half of the year, and long-term bond yields will follow by a comparable amount.
He said that the Fed won't ease in 1997 because the "cycle of weakness has past" and a rate cut would create the risk of financial markets "overshooting on the upside."
"Alan Greenspan doesn't want to be the first Fed chairman to preciptate two crashes in his term," Hoey said, adding that the Fed won't ease even if inflation remains tame.
As for municipal bonds, Richard Moynihan, head of tax-exempt fixed income, said the outlook for 1997 is not all that rosy.

He expects about $170 billion to $180 billion in new issuance next year -- similar to 1996 -- but with more regulations, legislation and the shifting of some spending to state and local governments from the federal government, munis will come under Still, he said, the mood of the market should remain "upbeat,' as state and local governments' financial positions remain positive.
